commit.message:
Whole-batch admission and grouped completion between connections and the committer (#76)

* Serve the client port with our own HTTP/2 gRPC server

Replace http.Server and grpc.Server.ServeHTTP with a server on x/net's
Framer and HPACK. Each connection has a reader and a writer goroutine;
unary calls still go through Node.Do. It serves every RPC etcdctl and
kube-apiserver use, /health and /version over HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1,
grpc-timeout, hasleader, RST_STREAM, flow control and GOAWAY.

Part of #50.

* Hand the node whole batches of requests and complete them per connection

The connection reader decodes every complete unary request that the node
runs and hands them to the node with one SubmitBatch call once the next
frame is not buffered, or at 256 requests or 4 MiB. The committer hands
each connection all of its replies of one turn in one Complete call, and
the writer encodes them. No goroutine, context, request struct or reply
channel per call is left on this path.

Part of #50.

* Format the raw-frame test with gofumpt

* Fix the review findings on the HTTP/2 server

A second END_STREAM resets the stream instead of running the call twice;
the writer gives each ready stream one frame per pass; control frames
are capped at 10,000; data past a stream's window resets it; contexts of
calls that end without a handler are released; HEAD gets no body.

* Use http.StatusOK in the HEAD check

* Fix the second review round on the HTTP/2 server

Every stream that requires a leader is watched for leader loss, not only
Watch; the node dropping a watch ends a send that waits for the client;
grpc-timeout ends a call at its deadline even before its request is
complete, and 0n counts; header blocks start with an HPACK table size
update to 0; padding is credited back to the stream.

* Fix the review findings on batch admission

A due batch is handed over before every frame read, stream errors and
continued header blocks included. Complete takes a lock of its own, so
the committer never waits on a connection. SubmitBatch refuses work once
the node stopped, and a stopping node's last replies are sent before the
calls it still held fail. Calls hold their request, a fixed cost and
their reply until the reply is sent; above 64 MiB the connection window
is not credited back, so the reader never blocks on it.

* Fix the third review round on the HTTP/2 server

A stream that ended takes no more messages, so a handler that runs on
after its deadline or leader loss cannot send DATA after the trailers.
Closing a connection stops its streams' deadline timers. A watch stream
is closed as too slow once 64 MiB of responses wait, not only at 4096.

* Format with gofumpt

* Keep a call's request and reply charges apart

A call holds its request charge from the batch handoff until the node
answers, and its reply charge until the reply is sent or reset, so a
deadline can no longer drop a charge the node still holds or leak one.
A call whose deadline passed before its batch goes out stays out.
Complete pushes onto a lock-free list instead of taking a mutex.

* Do not register a stream decoded after its connection closed

Its deadline timer would outlive the connection.

* Fix a lint finding in the close test

* Release request charges of retired calls when the node stops, and count waiting replies

The connection keeps the set of calls the node has not answered, so a
call that was reset or reached its deadline still has its request
charge freed when the node stops. Replies waiting for the writer count
against the connection's budget from the Complete handoff on.

* Count waiting replies until complete has charged them to their calls

takeCompletions dropped the waiting charge before the replies were
encoded and charged, so the reader could credit the window meanwhile.

@@ -201,7 +201,9 @@ Cost on this host (aarch64, 8 cores): about 80 ms per run of one seed, so 64 see
 
 **gRPC server.** `internal/server` serves the client port with its own HTTP/2 and gRPC code on x/net's Framer and HPACK, decided in the [design change on #50](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/50). grpc-go's server is not used; clients and tests still use grpc-go's client. It serves etcd's KV service (Range, Put, DeleteRange, Txn, Compact), Lease (Grant, Revoke, TimeToLive, Leases, and KeepAlive as a stream of one request at a time), Watch as described above, Cluster.MemberList and Maintenance.Status. Every other method of etcd's services, including RangeStream, Auth and member changes, answers Unimplemented with grpc-go's message; Kubernetes 1.37 falls back from RangeStream on exactly that code. Status reports version 3.7.2, storage version 3.7.0, the leader, the term, the commit and applied indexes, the 2 GiB default quota, "etcdserver: no leader" in Errors without a leader, and the estimated log size as the database size, never 0 because etcdctl divides by it.
 
-Each connection has a reader goroutine, which decodes frames and copies each request message once out of the Framer into a buffer of its own size, and a writer goroutine, which is the only one that writes and which keeps to the client's flow-control windows. A unary call runs in a goroutine of its own once its request is complete, calls `Node.Do`, and queues its reply; a streaming call runs in a goroutine from its first headers. Response header and trailer blocks are HPACK literals that are never indexed, each after a dynamic table size update to 0, so they are built once and are valid whatever table size the client set. The server follows grpc-go and etcd where clients can see it:
+Each connection has a reader goroutine, which decodes frames and copies each request message once out of the Framer into a buffer of its own size, and a writer goroutine, which is the only one that writes and which keeps to the client's flow-control windows. A streaming call runs in a goroutine from its first headers. Status and MemberList run in a goroutine of their own.
+
+The unary calls that the node runs (KV, Compact and the unary Lease calls) take the whole-batch path. The reader decodes each complete request and hands all of them to the committer with one `Node.SubmitBatch` call. It does this when reading the next frame could wait for the client, because that frame is not buffered whole or starts a header block that continues in later frames, or at 256 requests or 4 MiB. There is no timer. The committer submits each request to the core, and after each `Process` it hands every connection all of its replies of that turn with one `Complete` call. `Complete` only pushes them onto a lock-free list, adds their size (`proto.Size`, or a fixed estimate) to the connection's count of waiting replies, and wakes the writer, which encodes the replies. So such a call costs no goroutine, context, channel or inbox send of its own. Each call holds its request bytes plus 512 from when the reader hands it over until the node answers, and its reply bytes from then until the reply is sent or the client resets the call. A call whose deadline passed before its batch goes out is not handed over. Once a connection's calls and its waiting replies hold more than 64 MiB, its receive window is not credited back, so the client stops sending while the reader still reads pings, resets and window updates. If the node stops, every call it held fails with "server stopped" after the replies it already gave are sent. Response header and trailer blocks are HPACK literals that are never indexed, each after a dynamic table size update to 0, so they are built once and are valid whatever table size the client set. The server follows grpc-go and etcd where clients can see it:
 
 - The receive limit is etcd's 1.5 MiB request limit plus 512 KiB, with grpc-go's ResourceExhausted "received message larger than max". Compressed messages are refused with Unimplemented.
 - `grpc-timeout` ends the call with DeadlineExceeded when it passes, whether or not the request is complete or the handler started; `0n` has passed already. etcd's `hasleader` metadata fails a call without a leader with "etcdserver: no leader", unary calls included, and ends a Watch or LeaseKeepAlive stream after three checks one second apart find no leader, as etcd's interceptors do.
@@ -261,7 +263,6 @@ Later pieces plug in here without reshaping what exists.
 - **Responses prepared before commit.** `core.Node.apply` runs one entry against the index and answers its requests. To prepare responses before commit, the leader runs the same function on its proposals while they replicate, keeps the encoded replies, and releases them when the entry commits at the expected index and term. A leader change drops them. The followers keep applying at commit.
 - **Other transports.** The core only produces and consumes `raftpb.Message` values, and `node.Node` only needs a `peer.Transport` for sending and `Node.Deliver` for receiving. A tournament transport implements those two.
 - **The rest of the API.** Auth, Defragment, Snapshot, HashKV, Alarm and member changes stay Unimplemented; Kubernetes does not use them.
-- **Whole-batch frontend.** The connection reader is where the whole-batch write path of #50 starts: it can hand the committer every complete request of one read as one batch, instead of one goroutine and one `Node.Do` per call.
 - **Backpressure.** With 64 persist batches waiting, the committer takes no new inputs. A peer connection then blocks in `Node.Deliver` once the inbox of 8192 inputs is full, and client requests wait in `Node.Do`.
 - **Membership details.** MemberList reports client URLs only for the node that answers, because nodes do not tell each other their client URLs yet; `etcdctl --cluster` and clientv3's `Sync` see one endpoint. `--listen-client-urls`, `--advertise-client-urls` and `--listen-peer-urls` take one URL each, where etcd takes lists; a list is refused with an error.
